statement: The supplied sources contain no derivation, as a sparse matrix is a mathematical definition and computational object rather than a derived result. A sparse matrix (or sparse array) is defined as a matrix in which most of the elements are zero, commonly characterized by the criterion that the number of non-zero elements is roughly equal to the number of rows or columns, with sparsity defined as the ratio of the number of zero-valued elements to the total number of elements (m × n).

properties.property: The sparsity of an m × n matrix equals the count of zero-valued elements divided by the total number of elements m × n.
properties.why: It defines the proportion of zero elements in the matrix.

properties.property: A band matrix has lower bandwidth p if a_{i,j} = 0 whenever i > j + p, and upper bandwidth p if a_{i,j} = 0 whenever i < j - p.
properties.why: Non-zero entries are confined within a band around the main diagonal.

properties.property: An n × n diagonal matrix is an extreme band matrix with zero upper and lower bandwidth that requires only n memory entries as a 1D array.
properties.why: All elements outside the main diagonal vanish.

properties.property: The Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format represents an m × n matrix using three 1D arrays: V of length NNZ, COL_INDEX of length NNZ, and ROW_INDEX of length m + 1.
properties.why: Row indices are compressed while allowing efficient row slicing and matrix-vector products.

properties.property: The CSR format saves memory over dense storage only when NNZ < (m(n - 1) - 1) / 2.
properties.why: The combined length of the three CSR arrays (2 * NNZ + m + 1) must be strictly less than m * n.

properties.property: The Compressed Sparse Column (CSC) format stores values column-first with arrays (val, row_ind, col_ptr).
properties.why: Column index information is compressed relative to COO to allow efficient column slicing and arithmetic.

properties.property: Matrix factorizations can produce fill-in (entries changing from zero to non-zero), which can be reduced by row and column permutations.
properties.why: Elimination steps in algorithms such as Cholesky or QR factorization introduce non-zero values into previously zero locations.

assumptions.assumption: The matrix contains predominantly zero elements, commonly with NNZ roughly on the order of m or n.
assumptions.breaks_when: Most elements are non-zero (dense matrix), which causes sparse structures to incur higher memory and computational overhead than standard dense arrays.

assumptions.assumption: The number of non-zero entries satisfies NNZ < (m(n - 1) - 1) / 2 when stored in CSR format.
assumptions.breaks_when: NNZ >= (m(n - 1) - 1) / 2, causing CSR storage (2 * NNZ + m + 1 entries) to exceed or match the storage of a dense m × n matrix.

failure_modes.signature: Memory consumption explodes and operation counts increase drastically during Cholesky or QR decomposition.
failure_modes.cause: Zero entries transition to non-zero values during algebraic factorization without bandwidth minimization or row/column permutations.

failure_modes.mode: Memory and performance degradation on insufficiently sparse matrices
failure_modes.signature: Sparse matrix algorithms take longer to execute and consume more memory than dense algorithms.
failure_modes.cause: Sparse formats like CSR are applied to matrices where the number of non-zeros exceeds efficiency thresholds such as NNZ >= (m(n - 1) - 1) / 2.

failure_modes.signature: Slow running times during element insertions or matrix assembly.
failure_modes.cause: Constructing or modifying the non-zero structure directly in static compressed formats (CSR or CSC) instead of construction formats (DOK, LIL, or COO).
